15.24.1.en: "The LORD will destroy the house of the proud: but he will establish the border of the widow" [25]

15.24.2.en: It is not said of God that He resists any particular class of men except the proud (1 Pet 5:5). Here he affirms that He uproots them as from their very roots, since they bear the spirit of the devil, who by his pride wanted to set himself up as a god to be worshipped, to whom all creation would submit.

15.24.3.en: He who resists the proud, who rely on their abilities, their powers and their authority, takes care of the borders of the widow, which many covet in order to rob her of her rights and seize her possessions. He is the Judge of the widows, the Father of the fatherless, and the Defender of the wronged, the persecuted and the humiliated.

15.25.0.en: "The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD: but the words of the pure are pleasant words" [26]

15.25.1.en: If God hates the sacrifices and offerings presented by the wicked who persist in their evils, then it is fitting for them to give up their evils and their defiled thoughts, which the Holy One cannot bear.

15.25.2.en: God hates evil thoughts, and delights in the words of His holy children, and receives them as pure, acceptable thanksgiving hymns, well pleasing to Him.

15.25.3.en: * If the evil word is an abomination to the Lord your God, how much more the evil word that denies (the faith) and openly proclaims another god, and the evil oath.

15.25.4.en: * We are not harsh toward those who repent. Rather, the wicked are wicked to themselves, for whoever is ignorant of instruction hates himself. Yet we must seek healing for them in every possible way, even for the person who has turned completely aside and no longer feels his evils, but is drunk with an intoxicant more dangerous than wine, the intoxicant that arises from the darkness of evil.

15.26.0.en: Origen "He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live" [27]

15.26.1.en: The house signifies the Church. He troubles it who turns it from its spiritual mission to commercial business, or from its holiness, as Achan the son of Carmi troubled all the people of God (Josh 7:25).

15.26.2.en: Perhaps he refers here to judges and witnesses, since love of money sometimes plays a grave role in those of them who are perverted, so that they judge or bear false witness for the sake of gifts or bribes offered to them, with no regard for the feelings and fates of the wronged.

15.27.0.en: "The heart of the righteous studieth to answer: but the mouth of the wicked poureth out evil things" [28]

15.27.1.en: The righteous man is not hasty in speech, but gives his heart or mind the opportunity to study the matter so as to give a wise and truthful answer. The wicked, however, speak rashly without thought or deliberation, because what concerns them is their material or moral gains.

15.27.2.en: The righteous man fears the Lord, not men, so he weighs every word with all care, lest he anger God or wrong anyone.

15.28.0.en: "The LORD is far from the wicked: but he heareth the prayer of the righteous" [29]

15.28.1.en: St. Peter the Apostle quoted the Psalmist's saying: "For the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, and his ears are open unto their prayers: but the face of the Lord is against them that do evil" (Ps 34:15-16; 1 Pet 3:12). Truly God hears everything and sees everything, but the wicked are not worthy to be the object of God's knowledge, His sight and His hearing. They become as though far from Him, for there is no fellowship between the Holy One and evil!

15.28.2.en: * Wretched is the man who has masks for evil, and happy is the man who has many masks for goodness.

15.28.3.en: * "The wicked are like the dust which the wind scatters" (Ps 4:1). The Holy Scripture says that the wicked man will be wretched, so that he will not be even as the dust of the earth. For dust seems to have no existence, yet it surely has a kind of existence in itself... It is scattered here and there and has no one place, but the wind sweeps it away, and it has no power to resist. The same is true of the wicked man. As soon as he denies God, the breath of Satan sweeps him away into error and casts him wherever it wishes.

15.28.4.en: St. Jerome * God will receive those who repent, and will punish those who remain in their sins.

15.29.0.en: "The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart:

15.29.1.en: and a good report maketh the bones fat" [30]

15.29.2.en: Painful news spoils a person's peace and takes away his inner joy, and affects even his bodily health. But joyful news in the Lord refreshes the soul, and strengthens the bones of man, that is, his inner temple, and affects even his health.

15.29.3.en: The expression "fatness of the bones" is contrasted with "dryness of the bones," and it suits countries that depend on rain: if drought occurs the land loses its prosperity, famine befalls it, and it may be struck by diseases. So fatness of the bones signifies prosperity, refreshment and an abundance of good things.

15.30.0.en: 31 The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise. 32 He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding.

15.30.1.en: "The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise" [31]

15.30.2.en: The first word in the Ten Commandments is "Hear," so he who is careful to listen to the voice of truth is qualified to join the choir of the wise.

15.30.3.en: Listening in a spirit of obedience is bound up with wisdom.

15.31.0.en: "He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding" [32]

15.31.1.en: The proud man who does not accept discipline does not despise his counselors but despises himself, and treats his eternity lightly. But he who receives words of criticism with great attention gains understanding and knowledge.

15.31.2.en: * O the happiness of him who puts his will to death, and leaves the management of his soul to the one whom God has given him as father and teacher, for his place will be at the right hand of Jesus Christ the Crucified.

15.31.3.en: St. John Climacus * Satan sows evil in people by means of their hatred of guidance, and then they fall like leaves.

15.31.4.en: * If a man seeks counsel he discovers the plans of the enemy. And if he submits to guidance, Satan flees and will not be able to spread his nets. Therefore he always urges others not to submit to guidance and not to seek it.

15.32.0.en: "The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility" [33]

15.32.1.en: He concludes his discourse in this chapter with the fear of the Lord, which the humble receive, so that they obtain discipline and wisdom, and God honors them as He does men. It is as though the first and last lesson is to seek the fear of the Lord in a spirit of humility, so that we learn from God, who lifts up the humble.

15.32.2.en: * Humility is good at all times, and it delivers those who draw near to it from every distress.

15.32.3.en: The fruits of humility are many, and it begets many good things. From it perfection is born, and through it Noah was proved righteous before God and He saved him, as it is written that God said to him: "For thee have I seen righteous and perfect in thy generation" (see Gen 7:1).

15.32.4.en: St. Aphrahat * He wants us not to seize leadership for ourselves, but to reach the lofty heights through humility... O the greatness of humility, for (the humble soul) wins the indwelling of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

15.32.5.en: Fr. Theophylact * Humility lifted up Moses, but the proud were swallowed up by the earth.

15.32.6.en: * Put on humility at all times, and it makes you a dwelling place for God.

15.32.7.en: * Clothe yourself, my brother, with humility at all times, for it clothes your soul with Christ who gives it.

15.32.9.en: Carry me, that I may rejoice in You, O Wisdom of God!

15.32.10.en: * That I may possess You, O All-Compassionate, and enjoy long-suffering.

15.32.11.en: No wounding word will come out of my mouth to stir up the fires of wrath.

15.32.12.en: But it will be seasoned with the salt of Your Holy Spirit.

15.32.13.en: You will awaken in my soul, as in the souls of those who hear, the spirit of joy.

15.32.14.en: * Let my mouth be opened, and let my tongue speak what You pour into my heart.

15.32.15.en: Let every word come forth for the edification of my soul and the edification of my brethren, and let there be no place for foolishness on my tongue.

15.32.16.en: * As I speak I see You looking with love upon my words as upon my heart!

15.32.17.en: Your glances lift me up as to heaven.

15.32.18.en: Your eyes crush me with surpassing love.

15.32.19.en: * My tongue will utter only words of peace, for, being upright, it is sanctified by You and becomes like a tree of life, from which I pluck fruit for my soul!

15.32.20.en: Carry me by Your love, and discipline me according to Your mercy.

15.32.21.en: For You are my Father, all-wise and all-tender.

15.32.22.en: You shepherd me in Your wonderful pastures, You uphold me with Your rod and Your staff.

15.32.23.en: So I turn neither to the right hand nor to the left.

15.32.24.en: * I look into my depths, and I see You dwelling in them.

15.32.25.en: I see You as my treasure, which no one will take from me.

15.32.26.en: I see You shining upon me with the light of knowledge.

15.32.27.en: And You receive every act of worship from me as a pleasure to You.

15.32.28.en: You grant me Your righteousness that I may live by it, You fill me with heavenly joy, and my face becomes ever cheerful by the grace You give!

15.32.29.en: * You have turned my heart into a perpetual feast!

15.32.30.en: A feast of love toward You, and toward humanity.

15.32.31.en: * I see You ever at work in my life, removing from my heart the thorns of sloth and the briers of slackness.

15.32.32.en: You grant me the spirit of constant diligence, and growth without ceasing!

15.32.33.en: * That I may work by You and with You, I always seek the guidance of Your Holy Spirit.

15.32.34.en: And I bow in obedience to Your bride, the Holy Church.

15.32.35.en: By You I am humbled, for You are meek and lowly in heart.

15.32.36.en: * I was a widow for a long time, but You received my soul as Your bride, for You are the Judge of the widows and the support of the weak.

15.32.37.en: * Finally, what do I ask except that You grant me Your fear.

15.32.38.en: By Your fear I seek the wisdom that is with You.

15.32.39.en: By Your fear every loftiness and pride within me is brought down.

15.32.40.en: By Your fear my wilderness becomes a delightful garden, ever bearing the fruit of Your Holy Spirit!

16.0.s.en: 1. The Lord working in His believers

16.0.0.en: 1 The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD. 2 All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits. 3 Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established. 4 The LORD hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil.

16.0.1.en: "The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD" [1]

16.0.2.en: God sanctified freedom of will, and gave the rational creature the right of choice. It is man's right to choose the way, that is, the preparation of the heart and the intention, but it is God who grants the possibility and the power, even the possibility of answering with the tongue.

16.0.3.en: Without God man can do nothing, but He does not work in man by compulsion; rather, He leaves to him the choice of the way.

16.0.4.en: The prophet Jeremiah says: "O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps" (Jer 10:23). Even the human will, though we have received the right of choice, we need the grace of God that we may have strength of will, as the Apostle Paul says: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure" (Phil 2:13).

16.0.5.en: * Certainly, as it is written: "The preparation of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD" (Prov 16:10), some err from the way through lack of understanding, thinking that the preparation of the heart - that is, the beginning of goodness - belongs to man without the help of divine grace. Far be it from the children of the promise to understand it so.

16.0.6.en: * The horse does not tame itself, and neither can man do this. There is urgent need for man to tame the horse, and in the same way for God to tame man.

16.0.7.en: St. Augustine * God does not compel us, nor does the grace of the Spirit force our will, but God calls us and waits for us to come forward to Him in complete freedom, and when we draw near He grants us all His help.

16.0.8.en: * God does not compel those who do not want Him, but He draws those who want Him.

16.0.9.en: * God does not bind our desires or our will by His gifts, but no sooner do we begin and show readiness than we find Him offering us many opportunities for salvation.

16.0.10.en: * The Creator made our nature master of itself. In His mercy He always grants us His help, and He knows what is hidden in the depths of the heart. He entreats us, counsels us, forbids us and warns us against evil conduct, but He imposes nothing on us by force. He offers the suitable remedies, leaving the whole matter to the decision of the patient himself.

16.0.11.en: * We are masters; it is in our power to make every member of ours an instrument of evil or an instrument of righteousness.

16.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits" [2]

16.1.1.en: Since the fall of man, man has come to justify his behavior and give himself excuses, and to think that he is walking as is fitting, even if he realizes that what he does is wrong or a crime that he commits, but he reckons that circumstances have driven him to it. Therefore it was said: "The imagination of man's heart is evil" (Gen 8:21). "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" (Jer 17:9).

16.1.2.en: But if man accepts God's work in him, then he realizes that God's balances and reckonings are true, and he casts the blame on himself, not on the circumstances around him or on others, or on God Himself. For God does not err in His reckonings.

16.1.3.en: God grants His believers to enjoy the perception of His balances, not to crush them with grief and bitterness over their conduct, but to draw them to Himself, and so lift them up and sanctify them, and even glorify them.

16.1.4.en: Many of the Fathers of the Church, such as St. Clement of Alexandria and St. Basil the Great, called man to know the truth about himself, his inner depths, so that he may come to know God, who seeks his salvation, and to dwell in him.

16.1.5.en: * "Contemplate, then, yourself," until you reach the beholding of God.

16.1.6.en: * The Holy Scriptures warn you to pay great attention to yourself. So do not care for the body, nor for what is bound up with the body, such as health and beauty, pleasure and long life. Likewise do not pay great attention to wealth, glory and power, and all that is bound up with earthly life. But care for yourself above all things. For this is your precious treasure. Adorn it with the virtues, cleanse it from sin, and beautify it with the adornment of virtue, which is the most beautiful adornment. Contemplate well this thought: the body passes away and perishes, but the soul is immortal.

16.2.0.en: St. Basil the Great "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established" [3]

16.2.1.en: The Psalmist says: "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass" (Ps 37:5). If the Lord shatters the plans of the wicked against God and against the believers, on the other hand He gives assurance to His humble believers. He is a support to them in their plans and works as long as they are according to His divine will.

16.2.2.en: * The humble person shows us what is upright in no easy way. For the penitent person will not boast of great things. But God does not wish to know the works of the proud.

16.2.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * We were commanded to show our ways to Him, and to make them go toward Him, ways that become straight not by our own efforts but by His help and mercy. Therefore it is written: "Make thy way straight in my eyes," or as it stands in other copies: "Make my way straight in thine eyes," so that what is straight in His eyes may appear straight in mine. And Solomon says: "Open thy works before the Lord, and He will direct thy thoughts," for our thoughts are directed only when we meet before the Lord, as to a firm rock that is not shaken, and everything we do we attribute to Him.

16.3.0.en: St. Jerome "The LORD hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil" [4]

16.3.1.en: Though all the heavenly and earthly creation glorifies God the Creator who cares for His creation, yet He did not create it out of need of someone to glorify Him, but created it because of His goodness, His love and His giving to others.

16.3.2.en: He proclaims all the more His love and care on the great day of the Lord, when the spiritual believers enjoy the eternal inheritance, while the wicked are judged by their own evil to eternal destruction.

16.3.3.en: By saying: "He made all things for himself," the believer feels his value, that God created him for Himself, not to profit from him, nor out of need of him, but because He loves him, wants to bring him into His embrace, and to have him belong to Him, so that He says: "I am the God of Abraham..."

16.3.4.en: The believer feels that he is not a person among a throng of human beings numbering billions, but a man of God, very dear to Him, and cared for by Him personally.

16.3.5.en: A man often thinks that the law of the world is chaos and lawlessness, and that the law of the jungle and violence prevails. But in the midst of all that seems as if God's eyes do not watch over men, and as if God does not care about their conduct, there is a divine plan that is surely being fulfilled, and with certain success at the appointed time.

16.3.6.en: * These things... though in appearance they point to one aim and one end (for they urge us to keep away from unseemly things), yet they differ among themselves in loftiness. For faith and hope are more fitting for those who have not yet acquired the love of virtue as they aim toward goodness. But love belongs to God, and to those who have received within them to be in the image and likeness of God. For God alone does good neither out of fear nor out of desire for a word of thanks or the receiving of a reward, but does good simply for the love of goodness. This is as Solomon says: "The LORD hath made all things for himself" (Prov 16:4). By His goodness He pours out good on the worthy and the unworthy, for He is not moved to anger by faults, nor affected by the passions of men's sins, since He is always wholly good and unchangeable.

16.3.7.en: Fr. Cherimon * God is good, perfectly good, He alone, and since you are His image it is fitting for you to be good. He is generous to all, so you ought to be generous, avoiding greed, and not begrudging your neighbor anything material that passes away, for this is the greatest calamity and folly.

16.4.0.en: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD:

16.4.1.en: though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished" [5]

16.4.2.en: Those who walk in a spirit of pride isolate themselves from God, who in His humility created man, set him up as king, and gave him authority over the earth. Man's loftiness makes him lose his attachment to God, the source of all good things, and puts himself in the position of an adversary of God, and he thinks he is able to enter into contention with Him as an equal, and so he is not unpunished.

16.4.3.en: * Nothing is more foreign to the mercy of God, and nothing sends to the fires of hell like the tyrant of pride. If we possess it within us our whole life becomes defiled, even if we practice chastity, virginity, fasting, prayer, almsgiving and any virtue. Scripture says: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD." So we must examine this loftiness of soul, and cut off this cancer, if we want to be pure and be delivered from the punishment prepared for Satan.

16.4.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * It is shown with clear firmness, by examples and testimonies from Holy Scripture, that the sin of pride, although it is late in its order (among the sins), is the first of sins and faults, and it is not put to death by the virtue opposed to it (humility), and at the same time it destroys all the virtues, and tempts not only ordinary and simple people, but even more those who stand at the summit of courage.

16.4.5.en: For this reason the Apostle speaks of this spirit... and likewise the blessed David, although he was most careful of the storehouses of his heart to the point that he dared to address God, from whom the secrets of his conscience (his inner secrets) are not hidden, as in Ps 130 (131):1-2; Ps 100 (101):1-2. Nevertheless, since he knew the difficulty of watchfulness even for the perfect, he did not rely on his own efforts, but prayed to God and asked His help, so that he might come out victorious from the blows of his enemy, saying: "Plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me. Take hold of shield and buckler, and stand up for mine help" (Ps 35:1-2). And because he feared and trembled lest he fall into what was said about pride, he therefore says: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble" (Jas 4:6), "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD: though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished" (Prov 16:5).

16.4.6.en: St. John Cassian * We read of a thing like this in the book of Chronicles concerning Joash king of Judah. When he was seven years old Jehoiada the priest called him to become king, and by the testimony of Holy Scripture he was praised for all his works during the life of the aforementioned priest, but we hear of him after the death of Jehoiada how he was puffed up with pride and was delivered over to a more shameful state. "Now after the death of Jehoiada came the princes of Judah, and made obeisance to the king. Then the king hearkened unto them. And they left the house of the LORD God of their fathers, and served groves and idols: and wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this their trespass" (2 Chr 24:17-18). It was said a little later: "And it came to pass at the end of the year, that the host of Syria came up against him: and they came to Judah and Jerusalem, and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people, and sent all the spoil of them unto the king of Damascus. For the army of the Syrians came with a small company of men; and the LORD delivered a very great host into their hand, because they had forsaken the LORD God of their fathers. So they executed judgment against Joash. And when they were departed from him, (for they left him in great diseases,)" (2 Chr 24:23-25).

16.4.7.en: Behold, you see how the lust of pride delivered him to shameful lusts of uncleanness because he was puffed up with pride and allowed himself to be worshipped as a god, as the Apostle says: "For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections... God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient" (Rom 1:26, 28), and because Scripture says: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Prov 16:5). He who is puffed up with ever-increasing pride of heart is delivered over to great disgrace and shame, to be deceived by them.

16.4.8.en: So when he is humbled he must know that he has been soiled by the uncleanness of the flesh and the knowledge of unclean lusts, a thing he refused to know when he was in the pride of his heart. Also this shameful corruption of the flesh can expose the hidden defilement of the heart which was bound to it through the sin of pride, as though the visible corruption of his body could prove his pollution which he did not see before, so that he knows that he has become unclean through the pride of his spirit.

16.4.9.en: St. John Cassian * Yes, those who speak the words of God before God understand that they have received the words of teaching from God, and so they must seek to please God and not to please themselves. Likewise they must listen to the saying of Scripture: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Prov 16:5). It is clear that when these seek their vainglory by exploiting the word of God, they usurp the right of God, the Giver and Bestower, for they do not fear to rob of praise those who have received instruction in holy things. Let them hear also what Solomon says to teachers: "Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well. Let not thy fountains overflow outside, nor streams of water in the streets; let them be thine own alone, and not strangers' with thee" (Prov 5:15-17). When the teacher examines the depths of his heart and listens to what it says, he drinks from his cistern. And he drinks of the running waters from his well if he is moved by being watered from the spring of the Word. And when he added: "Let not thy fountains overflow outside, nor streams of water in the streets," he means that the shepherd should drink first and only then water others with teaching. The overflowing of the fountains outside is nothing other than the pouring out of teaching like water with power into others. And "streams of water in the streets" means the distribution of the divine word among great crowds of hearers, each according to his character. And because vainglory thrusts itself in as the word of God extends to the knowledge of many, the fitting saying came: "Let them be thine own alone, and not strangers' with thee." In this connection Wisdom calls the evil spirits "strangers." The prophet wrote of the tempters, saying: "For strangers are risen up against me, and oppressors seek after my soul" (Ps 54:3). Therefore he says that the streams of water in the streets should be yours alone, and this means that "it is necessary for the shepherd to go out to teach like streams in the streets, but he must not ally himself with the unclean spirits through conceit. We must not take enemies as partners in the service of the divine word." We must therefore spread our teaching far, that it may extend, without being tempted by any desire for vain praise.

16.5.s.en: 3. Love of God and of men

16.5.0.en: "By mercy and truth iniquity is purged: and by the fear of the LORD men depart from evil" [6]

16.5.1.en: By saying "by mercy and truth" he urges us toward repentance, or return to God, who is all-merciful, and in whom is all truth. We return to Him, and enjoy the fellowship of His attributes, and our iniquities are forgiven us by the precious Blood.

16.5.2.en: The fear of the Lord leads us in the way of truth, so that we turn neither to the right hand nor to the left, but remain firm in righteousness, as He is the Truth, the Giver of righteousness and holiness.

16.5.3.en: * The Holy Spirit speaks in the Holy Scriptures and says: "By alms and faith iniquity is purged" (cf. Prov 16:6), certainly not those sins that were committed before, for these are forgiven by the Blood of Christ and His sanctification.

16.5.4.en: And again he says: "Water will quench a flaming fire; and alms maketh an atonement for sins" (Sir 3:33). Here he makes clear that just as the fire of hell is quenched by the water of salvation, so by almsgiving and righteousness the flame of sins is put out (for those who believe in the Blood). Since in Baptism the forgiveness of sins is given once for all sins, the continual work without interruption - following the example of Baptism - grants the mercies of God again.

16.5.5.en: The Lord also taught us this in the Gospel, for when it was pointed out to Him that the disciples were eating without washing their hands, He answered, saying: "Did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also? But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you" (Lk 11:40-41). He teaches the washing of the heart, not of the hands, and that rather the uncleanness of the inside is to be removed, not the filth of the outside, and that when the mind is purified, then a man begins to cleanse his body. And as He counsels us how to wash and purify, He said that giving alms is necessary.

16.5.6.en: He who is tender teaches us and urges us to show compassion. For since He seeks the salvation of those for whom He offered such a sacrifice, He also pointed to those who, after receiving the grace of Baptism and committing sin, can be cleansed anew.

16.5.7.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr * Also with mercy and faith offenses are blotted out, for "by mercy and truth iniquity is purged" (Prov 16:6). And often this comes through our longing, striving and labor for the salvation of those who were saved by our warnings and exhortation, as Scripture says: "Let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins" (Jas 5:20).

16.5.8.en: Fr. Pinufius * My beloved... many times I remind you and confess to you what astonishes me greatly in what is recorded in Holy Scripture, and which I must often call to your attention.

16.5.9.en: I beseech you to consider what our Lord Jesus Christ said about Himself, that when He comes on the Day of Judgment, at the end of the world, He will gather all the nations before Him, and divide men into two parts: one part on His right hand and the other on His left.

16.5.10.en: He says to those on the right: "Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." But to those on the left He says: "Depart from me... into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels."

16.5.11.en: Inquire into the cause of this great reward or this dreadful punishment... Why do the first inherit the Kingdom? "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." And why do the others go into the eternal fire? "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat"...

16.5.12.en: The Lord did not say to these: "Come, inherit the Kingdom, for you lived pure, you deceived no man, nor wronged a poor man, nor encroached on anyone's borders, nor deceived anyone by an oath"...

16.5.13.en: But He said: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat." O the pre-eminence of almsgiving over all the other virtues, for the Lord did not point to all of them but to it alone!

16.5.14.en: Likewise He says to the others: "Depart into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels," and although there are many things He could raise against the wicked when they ask Him: "Why do we go into everlasting fire?" yet He does not answer them: "Why do you ask thus, you fornicators and murderers and deceivers and temple-robbers and blasphemers and unbelievers?"... But He says to them: "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat."

16.5.15.en: I see that you marvel as I do, and truly it is a marvelous thing, for it is written: "Water will quench a flaming fire; and alms maketh an atonement for sins," "Shut up alms in thy storehouses, and it shall deliver thee from all evil. Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and visit thy sins with alms" (cf. Sir 3:33; 9:15).

16.5.16.en: There are many testimonies from the divine inspiration in which appears how great are the benefits of charity in quenching sins and removing them, therefore charity will be attached to those whom God is about to judge, nay rather, it will crown them. It is as though He says to them: It is not difficult for Me to find a cause against you to condemn you when I examine you and weigh you accurately and scrutinize your works, but enter the Kingdom, for I was an hungred and you gave Me meat; you will enter the Kingdom not because you have not sinned, but through your charity you have removed your sins.

16.5.17.en: Likewise, as if He were saying to the others: Depart into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels... It is not because of the sins you think of, but because I was an hungred and you gave Me no meat; had you turned away from these evil deeds of yours, and turned to Me, you would have been saved from all your crimes and sins by your charities. For "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Mt 5:7). But now depart into everlasting fire, "for he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy" (Jas 2:13).

16.5.18.en: St. Augustine * Because you have not had mercy on others, no mercy shall be shown to you either, and because you shut the door of your house against the poor, God will not open to you the door of His Kingdom...

16.5.19.en: If you have fled from mercy, mercy flees from you. And if you have rejected the poor, He who became poor out of love for you rejects you.

16.6.0.en: 7 When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him. 8 Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right. 9 A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.

16.6.1.en: "When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him" [7]

16.6.2.en: True goodness, which is the fruit of the work of God's grace in man, has the power to love even enemies and win them to our side, so long as we offer it for the glory of God.

16.6.3.en: It was not possible for Laban to do evil to Jacob, for God Himself appeared in a dream of the night, "and said unto him, Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad" (Gen 31:24). As for Esau, who wanted to kill him, it was said of him: "Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept" (Gen 33:1-4).

16.6.4.en: * Wonderful is the goodness of the Lord. When God saw that Laban had inclined to make war on the good man and to enter into conflict with him, He said to him, as one reviewing his intention by the word: Take heed lest you become guilty by evil words against Jacob. Do not try to trouble Jacob even with a word, but take heed to yourself. Review this evil attack on your part. Control your anger. Control your raging thoughts, refrain from troubling him even with a word. I ask you to notice the compassions of God, for instead of commanding Laban to return to his place He directed him not to utter harsh or violent words against the good man. Why did this happen on earth? That the truly good man might learn, by truth and by experience, how far God cares for him.

16.7.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right" [8].

16.7.1.en: If a man's income is bound up with exploiting his brethren, it is bound up with the sin of cruelty, and he loses peace of heart, and so feels no happiness. For man's happiness does not rest on man's material possibilities, or his position or his authority, but on his union with the Holy One, and his enjoyment of the blessed life.

16.7.2.en: For the sake of a good conscience, and of present peace, and of the blessedness to come eternally, it is better for a man to gain a little to live on, by a lawful way, than to gain much by the evil ways of the world.

16.7.3.en: Let us not judge a man by his outward appearance, but according to his inner conscience. And let us strive to attain the virtue and happiness that come from works of righteousness and goodness. And would that we all - rich and poor - would imitate Lazarus, for this man endured the trials of virtue not once or twice or three times but many times, and I mean how he was poor and sick and had no one to help him, and was cast down at the door of a house that could have given him rest and relieved him of all his troubles, but did not give him a single word of comfort, and he saw the man who neglected him enjoying such luxury, and not only living in the enjoyment of this luxury, but also living in evils without suffering any trials or distress, and he did not look at or care for any other poor man like Lazarus, nor bring rest to himself with any thought of the resurrection. And besides these misfortunes he had a bad reputation among the crowds of people because of the trials that befell him. And not for a day or two or three, but all his life he saw himself in this state and saw the rich man in the opposite.

16.7.4.en: What excuse shall we have when this man bore all these calamities at one time and with such courage, if we do not bear even half of this?

16.7.5.en: * The fornicator or adulterer or thief, not only when he is accused, but even when he hears of others accused of the same crimes, imagines himself in the same punishment for his sins, and so takes a lesson from the punishment of others. Another has been condemned, but this one who has not been condemned is troubled because he dared to commit the same sins, and this also in the case of good works, when some receive praise and honor, those who have done the same good works rejoice and are glad, imagining themselves in this same honor. Do you think there is anyone more wretched than this sinner who, when he sees others accused, slips away to hide? And on the other hand, is there anyone happier than the righteous person when he sees other righteous men honored? For he rejoices and is glad, remembering his own good deeds amid the joy and exultation over the others.

16.8.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps" [9].

16.8.1.en: Man's heart is moved with a strong desire to think about achieving what is in his intention. With all the freedom of will that man has, he will not be able to move without God's care or God's permission. God created man a rational being, not that man should conceal this gift, but that while he plans he should lean on the breast of God and trust in Him, yet not in lack of thought or lack of movement toward work. As the Apostle Paul says: "Now God himself and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way unto you" (1 Thess 3:11).

16.8.2.en: * Do we still dare to boast of free will and insult the blessings of God, the Giver of gifts, if the chosen vessel (Paul) writes plainly: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" (2 Cor 4:7)?

16.8.3.en: St. Jerome * Paul did not work in order to receive grace, but he received grace in order to strive.

16.8.4.en: * How then can God's commandment be fulfilled, even with difficulty, without His help, since unless the Lord build the house, they labor in vain that build it.

16.8.5.en: St. Augustine * Paul wishes to remind us that we are not saved merely by our receiving God's free grace. Rather we must prove that we want to receive this free grace. The children of Israel received it, but they proved themselves unworthy of it and so were not saved.

16.9.s.en: 5. The obligation of the king or leader

16.9.0.en: 10 A divine sentence is in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment. 11 A just weight and balance are the LORD'S: all the weights of the bag are his work. 12 It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness. 13 Righteous lips are the delight of kings; and they love him that speaketh right. 14 The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it. 15 In the light of the king's countenance is life; and his favour is as a cloud of the latter rain. 16 How much better is it to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver!

16.9.1.en: "A divine sentence is in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment" [10]

16.9.2.en: It is fitting for the king or leader to realize his responsibility toward the people, for he is like one who represents God, and he must observe justice in his decisions, and seek not his personal advantage but the advantage of the people. It is fitting that he not make light of the word that comes out of his mouth.

16.10.0.en: "A just weight and balance are the LORD'S: all the weights of the bag are his work" [11]

16.10.1.en: However great a man's precision and honesty, it is hard for him to put things in their right place exactly, therefore the balance of truth belongs to the Lord.

16.10.2.en: What does he mean by the weights of the bag? Perhaps he means the bag kept in the temple, in which are the exact weights by which the balances of men are regulated. Or perhaps the "bag" here refers to the bag that merchants carried and in which they put gold and silver and other metals that they acquired in the course of their trade.

16.10.3.en: If merchants are bound to honesty in their balances, and so is every believer, how much more the king, to whom it is fitting to represent God in his leadership and care of the people, so that he keeps to justice, especially with balances.

16.10.4.en: It is not fitting for merchants, nor for leaders, especially the king, to separate their honesty in dealing with others from their worship of God, who is righteous and just, and without blame.

16.10.5.en: It is not fitting for a man to cheat in the balances, measuring with two measures, one by which he measures for his loved ones and friends and family and himself, and another by which he measures for strangers and those who oppose him!

16.11.0.en: "It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness" [12]

16.11.1.en: Let the king know that his throne is established not by his military or material or popular resources, but by divine righteousness. It is fitting for him as a king not only not to practice evil - and this is within his power - but to count even the mere thinking of it a defilement he cannot bear. He hates evil whether it comes from the people or from his palace or from himself personally.

16.11.2.en: By this the king becomes a shadow of the Lord Christ, the Son of David, King of kings. Of whom it was said: "And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness" (Isa 16:5).

16.12.0.en: "Righteous lips are the delight of kings; and they love him that speaketh right" [13]

16.12.1.en: Just as the king (or leader) is bound not only not to commit evil, but to hate even the mere thinking of evil, whether for himself or for those subject to him, so it is fitting for him to rejoice in those who speak the truth and to love those who speak uprightness.

16.12.2.en: How hard it is for those who occupy high positions, whether in society or in the Church, not to be deceived by words of flattery coming from those around them or from the people!

16.12.3.en: The splendid example of this is the role played by Bishop Flavian to calm the Emperor Theodosius when the people of Antioch assaulted his statues and rebelled against him. On the advice of the priest John Chrysostom, the bishop traveled eleven hundred kilometers until he reached Constantinople to say to the Emperor: [Your crown, O lord of Rome and of the world, is splendid, and is a proof of your worthiness, but it signifies the generosity that conveyed it to you. As for the crown of your humanity, the credit for it goes to your wisdom alone. Men admire the glittering jewels on your brow. But how great will be their admiration of the victory you win over your heart... If you pardon the Antiochenes you will gain great glory that will not fall away with the passing of the ages... You will bring great crowds into the Christian religion, for they will say: Look at the Christian religion. It has quenched the wrath of a man who has no equal in the world!]

16.13.0.en: "The wrath of a king is as messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it" [14]

16.13.1.en: If it is the duty of the king not to think evil, and not to be affected by words of praise, but to seek words of truth and love upright words, then it is the duty of the people to realize that the king is a man who has his weaknesses, and in his hand is authority. If anyone provokes him he is exposed to death. It is fitting for a man to be wise and pacify the king, giving honor to whom honor is due.

16.13.3.en: "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.

16.13.4.en: Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.

16.13.5.en: For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same" (Rom 13:1-3).

16.13.6.en: "I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men;

16.13.7.en: For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour" (1 Tim 2:1-3).

16.13.8.en: * Pray for kings (and rulers) (1 Tim 2:2), and for authorities and princes, pray for all who persecute you and hate you, and for the enemies of the Cross, that your fruit may be manifest to all, and that you may be perfect in Him (Christ).
